rv.q: That sense of new ownership joyfully pervades this splendid production, which opened officially Thursday night at Broadway’s Theatre.
Even so, 1776 succeeds where it counts: It sustains a sense of suspense about events whose outcome we know going in.

This "1776" pulsates with energy, snaps with attitude and enlivens history, which take place mostly in the Chamber of the Continental Congress in Philadelphia as these colonial representatives argue about breaking ties with England and constructing what would eventually be a clearly imperfect union.
It's an absolute blast. It wins you over in minutes.
The most uncomfortable bit is when the Black actors are tasked with recreating slaves at auction, a jarring step that could have been done more artfully.
What’s different, of course, are the voices singing those songs and hashing those historical details, and in that, at least, the new 1776, co-directed by Jeffrey L.
Unfortunately, this choice, which genuinely makes the sedative of a show more interesting to look at and listen to, further locks its subjects into binary stereotypes.
Is this a grabby gimmick that smacks of virtue-signaling, or does it result in an inspired reinvention?
It has remembered the ladies. But it can’t make them live.
Instead we get subtracted value.

The show’s enduring achievement of making long-ago historical figures arguing over politics entertaining, coupled with the amazing sense of suspense of whether the Declaration of Independence will be approved, remains potent in this exuberant and affirmative iteration.
At nearly three hours with intermission, the machinations of the last days leading up to July 4 begins to drag, unhurriedly circling the inevitability of that final, deathless Declaration.
The passage is at once progressive and thrillingly patriotic, offering a timely reminder that those qualities needn’t be mutually exclusive.

One can quibble about many other things in this production – can anyone adequately explain the meaning of set designer Scott Pask’s final image – but there’s no question that “1776” speaks loudly and clearly to audiences in 2022.
Hearing their voices is worth the price of admission.
I count the effort of both creative teams largely if not entirely a success.
While the show ranges in its woolly late-1960s way, its ending is elegantly simple, as we see the real-life signatures of the men in a cascade of projected graphics.
None of these alterations enhance 1776; what’s more, Page and Paulus push the running time, which in 1969 was a shade over two intermissionless hours, closer to three.
But overall, this remodeling job is all too raucous and too much in competition with itself to leave any sort of cohesive impression.
Somehow, even with the novelty of the casting this history-making event wasn’t as heart-poundingly satisfying as in other, more conservative versions.
This inevitably casts a shadow over the actual signing of the Declaration of Independence, rendering it an anti-climax.
The result, while enjoyable, shows a fundamental lack of trust and understanding in material that they would see already does the work for them, if they just stopped to listen.
They haven't engaged with 1776 so much as they have marked it up with a highlighter, garishly underlining points that are obvious in the original text.
Beyond the nontraditional casting, there’s nothing very revolutionary about this lackluster “1776.”
If that’s what the creators were going for, this is a revolution worth seeing.
All of which left me wondering, Why is this show here?

cn.t: Critics are divided on this diverse, all-female/nonbinary revival of the 1969 musical. While many praise the fresh casting and vibrant performances, others find the production overly didactic and lacking a clear point of view beyond its concept.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
